title: Budget vs actual scorecard
summary: Measure how far each store is from its budget, flag the ones outside tolerance and count the misses.

blocks.text: At month end the regional manager opens one sheet: budget against actual for each store. A shortfall matters, but so does a big overshoot, because it can mean the budget was set badly or stock was pushed into one store.
You will work out each store's variance in K and in %, flag any store more than 5% away from budget, and count how many stores missed.

items: Objective: calculate variance and variance %, flag misses with ABS and count them with COUNTIF.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.text: Variance = actual minus budget. Positive means above budget and negative means below.
Variance % = variance divided by budget, times 100, rounded to 1 decimal place. It tells you how big the gap is compared with the size of the budget.
ABS removes the minus sign: ABS(-7.5) is 7.5. It measures how far from budget a store is, in either direction.
If the gap in either direction is bigger than the tolerance in I2, show Miss. The dollar signs lock the tolerance cell.
COUNTIF counts the cells in a range that match a condition. Here it counts how many flags say Miss.
Tip: without ABS, a store 9% below budget has -9, which is smaller than the tolerance of 5, and it would never be flagged.
Four questions on variance and flags. Type numbers without commas or the % sign, for example -9.

items: Variance = actual - budget, and variance % = variance / budget x 100.
ABS measures the size of a gap whichever direction it goes.
An IF with a tolerance cell flags the stores that are off plan.
COUNTIF(range,"Miss") counts how many stores missed.

blocks.text: Next: the capstone, a one-row-per-store scorecard that brings your lookup and conditional-sum skills together.

items.prompt: A store had a budget of 500K and an actual of 455K. What is the variance (actual minus budget), in K? Include the minus sign if it is negative.
items.answerHint: Number in K, with a minus sign if below budget

items.prompt: For the same store (budget 500K, actual 455K), what is the variance %, to 1 decimal place? Include the minus sign.
items.answerHint: Number, 1 decimal place, with a minus sign if below budget

items.prompt: Why does the flag formula use ABS(E2) in =IF(ABS(E2)>$I$2,"Miss","On track")?

options.label: So that a store far below budget (a negative %) is flagged just like one far above it
To round the variance to 1 decimal place
Because variance % can never be negative
To count the stores that missed

items.prompt: The flags in F2:F6 read Miss, On track, Miss, Miss, On track. What does =COUNTIF(F2:F6,"Miss") return?
